title: What a Root Has to Reach

scenes.visual: Title card 'What a Root Has to Reach' over a cartoon plant whose roots run into tan soil dotted with BLUE and GREEN dots. COLOUR MAP for both films: phosphate BLUE dots; nitrate and ammonium GREEN dots; nitrogen gas PALE GREY paired dots labelled 'N2'; phloem movement a GOLD arrow; Casparian strip a DARK RED band; carbon payment ORANGE tokens; soil tan, roots cream, fungal threads WHITE. Every number appears only as on-screen text. No molecular structures: labelled blocks and cartoons, all marked 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: A green plant builds most of its body from carbon dioxide and water. But it also needs elements from the soil. Why can't it make those?
scenes.visual: A young tree grows on screen; arrows labelled 'carbon dioxide' flow into the leaves and 'water' up from the roots. A small third arrow labelled 'mineral elements' rises from the soil, and a question mark pulses over it.
scenes.narration: A green plant builds most of its body from carbon dioxide and water. But it also needs elements from the soil. Why can't it make those?

scenes.tts: A green plant can build all the organic molecules it needs. Every amino acid, every lipid, every nucleotide, it makes for itself. You cannot do that; you must eat some of yours.
scenes.visual: Inside a leaf cell, labelled blocks 'amino acids', 'lipids', 'nucleotides' assemble one after another under the heading 'organic molecules'. A small human silhouette at right holds a plate labelled 'some amino acids and vitamins: must be eaten'.
scenes.narration: A green plant can build all the organic molecules it needs. Every amino acid, every lipid, every nucleotide, it makes for itself. You cannot do that; you must eat some of yours.

scenes.tts: But no plant can make an element. Each element in its body has to come in from outside. That is the one thing it cannot do for itself.
scenes.visual: The blocks break apart into small lettered tiles, element by element. A padlock icon stamps over a tile labelled 'make an element?' with a red cross.
scenes.narration: But no plant can make an element. Each element in its body has to come in from outside. That is the one thing it cannot do for itself.

scenes.tts: Seventeen elements are conventionally essential. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen come from carbon dioxide and water. The other fourteen are mineral nutrients. Most plants take them chiefly from the soil.
scenes.visual: Seventeen tiles line up. Three, labelled C, H, O, float up to a 'carbon dioxide and water' cloud; fourteen drop down to a 'soil' band. Counter on screen: '17 = 3 from carbon dioxide and water + 14 mineral nutrients, mostly from soil'.
scenes.narration: Seventeen elements are conventionally essential. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen come from carbon dioxide and water. The other fourteen are mineral nutrients. Most plants take them chiefly from the soil.

scenes.tts: How the plant gets each one depends on three things. The form the element is in. How far that form moves. And who can take it up. This film follows how far.
scenes.visual: The fourteen soil tiles spread out. Three labels appear in turn: 'form', 'how far it moves', 'who can take it up: plant or partner'. The middle label brightens; a ruler slides under the tiles.
scenes.narration: How the plant gets each one depends on three things. The form the element is in. How far that form moves. And who can take it up. This film follows how far.

scenes.tts: Start with phosphate. Here is a young root, a little behind its growing tip, in soil dotted with phosphate.
scenes.visual: Zoom to a cream root cross-section in tan soil scattered evenly with BLUE dots labelled 'phosphate'.
scenes.narration: Start with phosphate. Here is a young root, a little behind its growing tip, in soil dotted with phosphate.

scenes.tts: As the root takes phosphate in, the soil right around it runs low. Phosphate creeps through soil so slowly that little arrives from farther out.
scenes.visual: BLUE dots next to the root move into it; a paler ring with fewer BLUE dots (fewer, not none) forms around the root, labelled 'lower available phosphate: depletion zone (schematic)'. Farther BLUE dots jitter but barely drift inward.
scenes.narration: As the root takes phosphate in, the soil right around it runs low. Phosphate creeps through soil so slowly that little arrives from farther out.

scenes.tts: Root hairs help. Each is a tube grown out from a single surface cell. Hairs push into the spaces between soil particles, past the depleted zone.
scenes.visual: Thin cream tubes sprout from single surface cells and grow outward through the pale ring into the BLUE-dotted soil beyond, label 'root hairs'. BLUE dots near their tips flow in.
scenes.narration: Root hairs help. Each is a tube grown out from a single surface cell. Hairs push into the spaces between soil particles, past the depleted zone.

scenes.tts: Many plants reach farther with a fungal partner, called a mycorrhiza. Its threads, called hyphae, are thinner still. They run far out into the soil and bring phosphate back.
scenes.visual: WHITE threads branch from the root far beyond the hairs, labelled 'hyphae of a mycorrhiza (fungal partner)'. BLUE dots travel back along them to the root.
scenes.narration: Many plants reach farther with a fungal partner, called a mycorrhiza. Its threads, called hyphae, are thinner still. They run far out into the soil and bring phosphate back.

scenes.tts: Nitrate is a different story. It moves through soil far more readily, and water flowing toward the root carries it too. For nitrate, reach matters less.
scenes.visual: Split screen: GREEN dots labelled 'nitrate' stream toward a plain root from well beyond its surroundings, riding small blue water arrows; only a faint ring forms and it refills quickly from farther out. Caption: 'nitrate: reach matters less'.
scenes.narration: Nitrate is a different story. It moves through soil far more readily, and water flowing toward the root carries it too. For nitrate, reach matters less.

scenes.tts: Inside the plant, elements can move again. The phloem, the tissue that carries sugar, can move some of them out of old leaves. Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and magnesium are among them.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the whole plant. A GOLD arrow runs from the lower, older leaves up the stem toward the growing tip. Tiles 'N', 'P', 'K', 'Mg' ride the arrow, labelled 'mobile in the phloem'.
scenes.narration: Inside the plant, elements can move again. The phloem, the tissue that carries sugar, can move some of them out of old leaves. Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and magnesium are among them.

scenes.tts: Now suppose nitrogen runs short. Which leaves turn yellow first, the old ones or the young ones?
scenes.visual: Supply of GREEN dots at the root dwindles. The plant's leaves flicker; question card 'Nitrogen runs short. Old leaves or young leaves first?'
scenes.narration: Now suppose nitrogen runs short. Which leaves turn yellow first, the old ones or the young ones?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card holds; 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: The old ones. The plant pulls nitrogen out of its oldest leaves and sends it up to the growing tip. So the old leaves yellow first.
scenes.visual: The GOLD arrow carries nitrogen tiles upward; the oldest lower leaves fade from green to yellow while the top leaves stay green. Label 'old, lower leaves first'.
scenes.narration: The old ones. The plant pulls nitrogen out of its oldest leaves and sends it up to the growing tip. So the old leaves yellow first.

scenes.tts: Iron and calcium are different. Once laid down, they stay largely where they are. So a shortage of iron shows first in young leaves.
scenes.visual: Second plant beside the first: 'Fe' and 'Ca' tiles sit fixed in the old leaves, no GOLD arrow. The young top leaves turn yellow. Label 'young leaves first'.
scenes.narration: Iron and calcium are different. Once laid down, they stay largely where they are. So a shortage of iron shows first in young leaves.

scenes.tts: Treat these patterns as clues to test, not a key for every species. Different shortages can look alike.
scenes.visual: Both plants side by side; a magnifying glass passes over them with the label 'a clue, not a diagnosis'.
scenes.narration: Treat these patterns as clues to test, not a key for every species. Different shortages can look alike.

scenes.tts: So the plant faces one question again and again. It cannot make an element. How far does each nutrient move, and how will the plant reach it?
scenes.visual: Recap montage: the depleted ring with hairs and WHITE hyphae; GREEN nitrate drifting in; the GOLD arrow between leaves.
scenes.narration: So the plant faces one question again and again. It cannot make an element. How far does each nutrient move, and how will the plant reach it?

scenes.visual: End card with Hex. LINE: 'How far a nutrient moves shapes how a plant must reach it.'
